title: Which tasks of building a wood-frame house hold the crew hours, and which can a stock humanoid even hold the load for?
summary: An open task book of one small house (28×40 ft, one storey, 2×6 at 16 in, from house-framing's takeoff): 20 tasks across wall framing, wall and roof sheathing, insulation and drywall, each with cycles, mass handled, hand height, reach, a tolerance, minutes per unit and crew-hours, as CSV and JSON. Counts come from code (210 framing pieces, 32 wall and 46 roof sheets, 72 drywall sheets, 8,760 fasteners); masses from the lumber, sheet and tool figures of buildbot-payload; robot verdicts from its simulated G1 and H1 payload envelopes. Minutes per unit are my assumptions: no primary time study could be read from this session, so they are swept ×1/3 to ×3, and my framing rows come out 5.5× below the one cited norm I found (Methvin, 0.12 man-hours per metre of stud, read as a search snippet), shown as a second scenario. Total 46 crew-hours (40–77 over the sweep) for this scope, or 93 with framing at the norm. Fastening is the biggest verb (29% of the hours, 21% in the second scenario) and taping and sanding drywall the biggest task. The H1 passes the payload test for tasks holding 54–81% of the hours (57–85% in scenario B), the G1 only 6–22% (7–31%); roof and ceiling work sits outside both robots' reach envelope. A payload pass is not a skill: force, placement accuracy and perception are untested.
lede: which house-building tasks hold the crew hours, and which can a stock humanoid hold the load for? An open task book of a 28x40 ft wood-frame house: 20 tasks with cycles, masses, tolerances and crew-hours, scored against the simulated Unitree G1 and H1 payload envelopes; fastening is 31% of the hours, and the H1 passes the payload test for 53-81% of them (minutes per unit are assumptions, swept).
